'''George Wetherill''' (August 12, 1925 – July 19, 2006) was an American physicist and geologist. He was the director emeritus of the department of terrestrial magnetism at the [[Carnegie Institution of Washington]].<ref name="Pearce"/><ref name="George W. Wetherill">{{Cite web|title=George W. Wetherill|url=https://nationalmedals.org/laureate/george-w-wetherill/|access-date=2021-08-18|website=National Science and Technology Medals Foundation|language=en-US|archive-date=2021-11-17|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211117202339/https://nationalmedals.org/laureate/george-w-wetherill/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2000, Wetherill received the [[J. Lawrence Smith Medal]] from the [[National Academy of Sciences]] "For his unique contributions to the cosmochronology of the planets and meteorites and to the orbital dynamics and formation of solar system bodies."<ref name="Smith"/>
In 2003, Wetherill received the [[Henry Norris Russell Lectureship]], the highest honor bestowed by the [[American Astronomical Society]], "For pioneering the application of modern physics and numerical simulations to the formation and evolution of terrestrial planets."<ref name="Russell"/>

== Early life and education ==
George Wetherill was born on August 12, 1925, in [[Philadelphia]]. Wetherill benefited from the [[G.I. Bill]] to receive four degrees, the Ph.B. (1948), S.B. (1949), S.M. (1951), and Ph.D., in physics (1953), all from the [[University of Chicago]]. He did his thesis research on the spontaneous [[Nuclear fission|fission]] of [[uranium]], as well as nuclear processes in nature, as a [[United States Atomic Energy Commission|U.S. Atomic Energy Commission]] Predoctoral Fellow.<ref name="AIP">{{Cite web|title=Wetherill, George West - Niels Bohr Library & Archives|url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11611007.html|access-date=2021-08-18|website=American Institute of Physics|archive-date=2021-05-17|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210517201831/https://history.aip.org/phn/11611007.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Career and achievements ==
=== Department of Terrestrial Magnetism (1953–1960)===
After receiving his Ph.D., Wetherill became a staff member at Carnegie's Department of Terrestrial Magnetism (DTM) in Washington, D.C. There, he joined an interdepartmental group who were working to date rocks using geochemical methods that measured natural [[radioactive decay]]. This involved determining the concentration and [[Isotope|isotopic]] composition of [[inert gases]] such as [[argon]], as well as the isotopes of [[strontium]] and [[lead (element)|lead]].<ref name="Pearce"/>

Wetherill originated the concept of the Concordia Diagram for the uranium-lead isotopic system; this diagram became the standard means for determining precise ages of rocks, and of detecting the possibility of [[metamorphism]]. It provides a basis for high-precision [[geochronology]] of rocks dating back through the history of the planet Earth.<ref name="Pearce"/>

Wetherill was also a member of the Carnegie group that accurately determined the decay constants of [[potassium]] and [[rubidium]], an effort that has also become fundamental to the measurement of geological time.<ref name="Pearce">{{Cite news|last=Pearce|first=Jeremy|date=2006-07-28|title=George W. Wetherill, 80, Expert on Dating of Rocks, Dies|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/07/28/us/george-w-wetherill-80-expert-on-dating-of-rocks-dies.html|access-date=2021-08-18|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2021-11-17|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211117203839/https://www.nytimes.com/2006/07/28/us/george-w-wetherill-80-expert-on-dating-of-rocks-dies.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Wetherill">{{Cite journal|last=Wetherill|first=George W.|title=Contemplation of Things Past|journal=Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences|year=1998|language=en|volume=26|issue=1|pages=1–21|doi=10.1146/annurev.earth.26.1.1|bibcode=1998AREPS..26....1W|issn=0084-6597|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== University of California, Los Angeles ===
Wetherill left DTM in 1960 to become a professor of geophysics and geology at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]]. There, he served as chairman of the interdepartmental curriculum in geochemistry (1964-1968), and as chairman of the Department of Planetary and Space Sciences (1968-1972).<ref name="Holley"/>

At UCLA, Wetherill further explored techniques for age-dating, examining extraterrestrial material with radiometric chronology techniques to [[meteorite]] and [[Moon|lunar]] samples. At the same time, he began to theorize about the origin of meteorites. His studies concentrated on collisions between objects in the [[asteroid belt]] together with resonances between their motions and those of planets. He computed how these events could move material into Earth-crossing orbits to become meteorites or larger Earth-impacting bodies responsible for the devastating impacts that caused mass extinctions of the majority of living species, including the dinosaurs.<ref name="Holley"/>

Later, Wetherill, along with scientists elsewhere, proposed that a certain unusual class of meteorites was not asteroidal in origin but instead came from the planet [[Mars]]. This was later confirmed by laboratory work elsewhere and is now well accepted.<ref name="Holley">{{Cite news|last=Holley|first=Joe|date=2006-07-22|title=George Wetherill|language=en-US|newspaper=Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/2006/07/22/george-wetherill/e47f2f52-fd34-4da2-bdee-d92612b7a081/|access-date=2021-08-18|issn=0190-8286}}</ref>

=== Department of Terrestrial Magnetism (1975–1991) ===
In 1975, Wetherill returned to Carnegie's Department of Terrestrial Magnetism as director. He remained director until 1991, when he became a staff member. At DTM, he began extending his research efforts into questions concerning the origin of the terrestrial planets--[[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]], [[Venus]], [[Earth]], and [[Mars]]. He was stimulated by earlier studies by [[Victor Safronov]] (O. Yu. Schmidt Institute, Moscow), who showed that as a swarm of [[planetesimal]]s coagulated into large bodies the swarm could evolve to produce a few terrestrial planets. Wetherill developed a technique to calculate numerically the orbital evolution and accumulation of planetesimal swarms, and he used the technique to reach specific predictions of the physical and orbital properties of terrestrial planets. His results agreed well with present observations.<ref name="Henbest">{{Cite web|last=Henbest|first=Nigel|title=Science: Are there lots of Earths out there?|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg13117813-200-science-are-there-lots-of-earths-out-there/|access-date=2021-08-18|website=New Scientist|language=en-US|archive-date=2021-08-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210818051653/https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg13117813-200-science-are-there-lots-of-earths-out-there/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In addition to showing how the inner solar system formed, Wetherill's work provided the basis for a model of a giant-impact origin for the [[Moon]]<ref name="Melosh">{{cite journal |last1=Melosh |first1=H. J. |title=New approaches to the Moon's isotopic crisis |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences |date=13 September 2014 |volume=372 |issue=2024 |article-number=20130168 |doi=10.1098/rsta.2013.0168 |pmid=25114301 |pmc=4128260 |bibcode=2014RSPTA.37230168M }}</ref> and the core of Mercury.<ref name="Spalding">{{cite journal |last1=Spalding |first1=Christopher |last2=Adams |first2=Fred C. |title=The Solar Wind Prevents Reaccretion of Debris after Mercury's Giant Impact |journal=The Planetary Science Journal |date=1 March 2020 |volume=1 |issue=1 |page=7 |doi=10.3847/psj/ab781f |arxiv=2002.07847 |bibcode=2020PSJ.....1....7S |s2cid=211171488 |language=en |issn=2632-3338 |doi-access=free }}</ref> It also led to explanations for the isotopic abundances of present-day planetary atmospheres.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lupu |first1=R. E. |last2=Zahnle |first2=Kevin |last3=Marley |first3=Mark S. |last4=Schaefer |first4=Laura |author4-link=Laura K. Schaefer |last5=Fegley |first5=Bruce |last6=Morley |first6=Caroline |last7=Cahoy |first7=Kerri |last8=Freedman |first8=Richard |last9=Fortney |first9=Jonathan J. |title=The Atmospheres of Earthlike Planets After Giant Impact Events |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=28 February 2014 |volume=784 |issue=1 |page=27 |doi=10.1088/0004-637x/784/1/27 |arxiv=1401.1499 |bibcode=2014ApJ...784...27L |hdl=1721.1/92946 |s2cid=10033333 |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0004-637X/784/1/27 |access-date=12 May 2022 |language=en |issn=0004-637X |archive-date=12 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220512182018/https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0004-637X/784/1/27 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Wetherill has shown that [[Jupiter]] plays an important role in the evolution of the [[Solar System]]; by ejecting [[comets]] from the Solar System, it offers a protective presence to the inner planets.<ref name="Holley"/> Wetherill's theoretical work supports discussions on the origins of the Solar System as well as on [[extrasolar planets]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ksanfomaliti |first1=L. V. |title=Extrasolar Planetary Systems |journal=Solar System Research |date=1 November 2000 |volume=34 |issue=6 |pages=481–495 |doi=10.1023/A:1005218112981 |s2cid=117713002 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1023/A:1005218112981 |language=en |issn=1608-3423 |access-date=12 May 2022 |archive-date=12 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220512182021/https://link.springer.com/article/10.1023/A:1005218112981 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wetherill |first1=G. W. |title=The Formation and Habitability of Extra-Solar Planets |journal=Icarus |date=1 January 1996 |volume=119 |issue=1 |pages=219–238 |doi=10.1006/icar.1996.0015 |bibcode=1996Icar..119..219W |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0019103596900159 |language=en |issn=0019-1035 |access-date=12 May 2022 |archive-date=12 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220512182016/https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0019103596900159 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Community engagement===
Wetherill provided leadership in the scientific community by serving on advisory committees for [[NASA]], the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]],<ref name="NAS">{{Cite web|title=George W. Wetherill|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/george-w-wetherill-as990t/|access-date=2021-12-07|website=www.nasonline.org|archive-date=2021-12-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211207151630/http://www.nasonline.org/member-directory/deceased-members/49210.html|url-status=live}}</ref> and the [[National Science Foundation]]. For 15 years, he was editor of the ''[[Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences]]''.<ref name="Jeanloz">{{cite journal |last1=Jeanloz |first1=Raymond |title=Preface |journal=Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences |date=May 1997 |volume=25 |issue=1 |article-number=annurev.ea.25.092506.100001 |doi=10.1146/annurev.ea.25.092506.100001 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

He served as president of the [[Meteoritical Society]], the [[Geochemical Society]], the Planetology Section of the [[American Geophysical Union]], the International Association of Geochemistry and Cosmochemistry,<ref>{{Cite web|title=NASA - NASA ASTROBIOLOGY INSTITUTE MEMBER GEORGE WETHERILL HONORED|url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/ames/news/releases/2000/00_34AR.html|access-date=2021-08-18|website=www.nasa.gov|language=en|archive-date=2021-08-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210818051115/https://www.nasa.gov/centers/ames/news/releases/2000/00_34AR.html}}</ref> and was a member of the [[American Philosophical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=George+W.+Wetherill&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|access-date=2021-12-07|website=search.amphilsoc.org|archive-date=2021-12-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211207151632/https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=George+W.+Wetherill&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|url-status=live}}</ref>

Wetherill died at his home in [[Washington, D.C.]], on July 19, 2006, aged 80, after a long illness.<ref>{{Cite web|title=George Wetherill|url=https://www.lpi.usra.edu/features/wetherill/|access-date=2021-08-18|website=www.lpi.usra.edu|archive-date=2021-07-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210730143407/https://www.lpi.usra.edu/features/wetherill/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Obituary">{{cite news |title=Father of Earth-formation models, Carnegie's George Wetherill, dies at 80 |url=https://carnegiescience.edu/news/father-earth-formation-models-carnegie%E2%80%99s-george-wetherill-dies-80 |access-date=10 May 2022 |work=Carnegie Institution for Science |date=21 July 2006 |language=en |archive-date=9 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220709120518/https://carnegiescience.edu/news/father-earth-formation-models-carnegie%E2%80%99s-george-wetherill-dies-80 |url-status=live }}</ref>
